# 2 Maccabees Chapter 10 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 10 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_010_page_001.jpg

---

## Council Notes

**Chapter Overview:** The rededication of the Temple — the origin of Hanukkah (vv. 1-8). Note the deliberate eight-day parallel with the Festival of Booths (Sukkot). The narrative then pivots to wars against the Idumeans and Timothy. The divine apparition in vv. 28-29 (five horsemen with golden bridles) is typical of the author's epiphany-theology; compare 3:25, 5:2-4, 11:8.

**Key Decisions:**
- "Festival of Booths" / "Feast of Tabernacles": EMET uses "Feast of Tabernacles"; LOGOS/PNEUMA use "Festival of Booths" — consensus uses "Festival of Booths" as cleaner modern rendering
- Hanukkah notation (PNEUMA v. 8): PNEUMA adds parenthetical "(This is the origin of Hanukkah)" — useful but not in Greek text; omit in consensus
- "Bread of presentation" (v. 3): EMET uses "presentation of the bread," LOGOS "bread of presentation" — LOGOS preferred; technical liturgical term
- "Ivy-wreathed wands" (v. 7): all three agree; this is a significant detail — Sukkot palm/myrtle/willow branches were being replicated with what was available
- "Five magnificent men on horseback" (v. 28): EMET "resplendent," LOGOS "magnificent," PNEUMA "magnificent" — LOGOS/PNEUMA preferred
- "Cistern" vs. "pit" (v. 36): EMET "pit," LOGOS "cistern" — LOGOS correct; Greek *lakkon* = cistern/pit; "cistern" is more precise here

---

**10:1** Maccabeus and his men, with the Lord guiding their way, recovered the temple and the city.

**10:2** They tore down the altars that the foreigners had erected in the public squares, and likewise the sacred enclosures.

**10:3** After purifying the sanctuary, they built a new altar; then, striking fire from flints, they offered sacrifices for the first time in two years, burned incense, lit the lamps, and set out the bread of presentation.

**10:4** When they had done all this, they fell prostrate and implored the Lord that they might never again fall into such calamities, and that if they should ever sin, he would discipline them with clemency rather than deliver them over to blasphemous and barbarous peoples.

**10:5** On the very day on which the sanctuary had been desecrated by foreigners — the twenty-fifth of Chislev — on that same day the purification of the temple took place.

**10:6** They celebrated eight days with gladness, after the manner of the Festival of Booths, recalling that not long before, during the Festival of Booths, they had been living as wanderers in the mountains and caves after the manner of wild animals.

**10:7** Carrying ivy-wreathed wands and leafy branches and palm fronds as well, they offered hymns of thanksgiving to him who had brought the purification of his holy place to a successful completion.

**10:8** By public decree, ratified by vote, they ordained for the entire Jewish nation that these days should be observed every year.

**10:9** Such was the end of Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes.

**10:10** We shall now give an account of the events under Antiochus Eupator, the son of that impious man, summarizing the disasters that accumulated in the wars.

**10:11** When Eupator succeeded to the throne, he appointed a man named Lysias to oversee affairs of state, naming him commander-in-chief of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.

**10:12** Ptolemy, who was called Macron, had taken the lead in dealing justly with the Jews on account of the wrong done to them, and tried to maintain peaceful relations with them.

**10:13** As a result he was denounced before Eupator by the king's friends and heard himself called a traitor on every side — for having abandoned Cyprus, which Philometor had entrusted to him, and having gone over to Antiochus Epiphanes. Finding no honorable way out of his situation, he ended his life by poison.

**10:14** Gorgias, who had been appointed general of that region, maintained a force of foreign troops and at every opportunity prosecuted the war against the Jews.

**10:15** The Idumeans alongside him held certain strategically important strongholds and were harassing the Jews, sheltering the refugees expelled from Jerusalem and attempting to keep the war going.

**10:16** Maccabeus and his men made supplication to God and entreated him to be their ally, then launched their assault against the strongholds of the Idumeans.

**10:17** Attacking with vigor, they gained control of the positions, drove back all who fought on the walls, and cut down those they encountered, killing no fewer than twenty thousand.

**10:18** No fewer than nine thousand had fled into two towers that were extremely strong and well supplied with provisions for a siege.

**10:19** Maccabeus left Simon, Joseph, and Zacchaeus with sufficient forces to maintain the siege, and himself moved on to places requiring more urgent attention.

**10:20** The men with Simon, however, being lovers of money, were bribed by certain persons in the towers; having received seventy thousand drachmas, they allowed some of the defenders to escape.

**10:21** When a report of what had been done reached Maccabeus, he assembled the leaders of the people and accused those men of having sold their fellow countrymen for money by releasing their enemies to fight against them.

**10:22** He put these traitors to death and immediately took the two towers.

**10:23** Succeeding in everything through force of arms, he destroyed more than twenty thousand in those two strongholds.

**10:24** Timothy, who had previously been defeated by the Jews, assembled an enormous force of foreign troops and brought together a large cavalry from Asia, intending to seize Judea by force.

**10:25** As he drew near, Maccabeus and his men scattered earth on their heads and bound their loins with sackcloth, falling in supplication at the foot of the altar, entreating God to look on them with favor and to be an enemy to their enemies and an adversary to their adversaries, as the Law declares.

**10:26** After this prayer they took up their arms and advanced a considerable distance from the city; when they drew near the enemy, they halted.

**10:27** Just as dawn was breaking, the two armies engaged. The one side had as the pledge of their success not only their valor but their refuge in the Lord; the other took their own rage as their guide into battle.

**10:28** When the battle grew fierce, five magnificent men on horseback appeared to the enemies from heaven, with golden bridles, placing themselves at the head of the Jews.

**10:29** They positioned themselves around Maccabeus, covered him with their own armor, and kept him unharmed, while hurling arrows and thunderbolts against the enemy, so that they were thrown into confusion and blindness and thrown into utter disorder.

**10:30** Twenty thousand five hundred were killed, along with six hundred cavalry.

**10:31** Timothy himself fled to a stronghold called Gazara, a well-fortified place where Chaereas was in command.

**10:32** Maccabeus and his men besieged the fortress with rejoicing for four days.

**10:33** Those inside, trusting in the strength of the place, reviled them excessively and uttered abominable words.

**10:34** At the dawn of the fifth day, twenty young men from Maccabeus's company, burning with anger at the blasphemies, stormed the wall with manly boldness and fierce courage and cut down everyone they encountered.

**10:35** Others came up in the same way while the defenders were occupied with fighting those men; they set fire to the towers and kindled fires that burned the blasphemers alive; others broke open the gates, admitted the rest of the army, and seized the inner courts.

**10:36** Timothy had hidden in a cistern, but they found him and killed him along with his brother Chaereas and Apollophanes.

**10:37** When this was accomplished, they praised the Lord with hymns and thanksgivings — he who bestows great benefits on Israel and grants them the victory.

**10:38** A short time later, Lysias, the king's guardian and kinsman and administrator of the realm, came against Judea with a powerful force.
